clauses.requirement: The loopback exception to the https rule has one definition, and it agrees with what URL.hostname produces.

clauses.notes: Found by the Part 8 release-artifact audit, which turned up four copies of the predicate in the shipped bundle. Six places in source asked whether a host is the local machine, each in order to relax the https rule. Five were character-identical under three different names; the sixth, in checkNavigable, tested for ‘::1’ while URL.hostname produces ‘[::1]’, so its IPv6 case never matched and an IPv6 loopback page was treated as insecure. It failed closed, which is why nothing caught it. One isLoopbackHostname now, with a census asserting one definition and that the body appears nowhere else under any name. Consolidating loosens that one check — http://[::1] is now secure, as http://127.0.0.1 already was — and the predicate stays narrow of 127.0.0.0/8 and 0.0.0.0 on purpose, since a narrower answer refuses what a broader one would allow.

It read: "a named permission profile attached to a shortcut is a **stored permission with a name on it**", and the workflow and shortcut design turns on the opposite rule. That is true of exactly one reading — the *authority* reading — and three others were never evaluated. The reading adopted is **tightening only**. A profile resolves to a permission mode, and the effective mode for a dispatch is `strictestMode(ambient, floor)` — so a profile can make a run stricter than the current setting and can never make one looser, whichever direction the setting later moves. It grants nothing, and there is no value it could hold that grants anything. `SHORTCUT_PERMISSION_PROFILES` has one member because `manual` is the strictest mode this build has, so there is exactly one tightening to express. A user-defined profile store was rejected as a second authorization surface with nothing to add. An unrecognised name — including §50's own `"qa-default"` example — is **refused rather than ignored**, because ignoring one would leave a shortcut that reads as stricter than it is. The floor is on the durable task record and is read on every dispatch by `loadPolicyContext`, so it survives a worker eviction rather than being a fact about one worker generation. `strictestMode`'s ordering is declared as data rather than taken from `PERMISSION_MODES`, whose order is a declaration order — relying on it would let a reordering for display silently change what a profile does. The commutativity, idempotence and never-looser properties are asserted over every mode pair rather than the pairs somebody thought of.

clauses.requirement: A named server is stored without trust or credentials, its tools exist only as a function of a fresh answer, and removing it removes them.
clauses.note: The store owns two properties. Identity is unique — a duplicate id is refused rather than renamed or merged, because an id is part of every tool name the server contributes and resolving a collision silently would point a task's existing tool at a different endpoint. And a record has nowhere to put a credential: `validateServerDescriptor` produces exactly three fields and `isStorableServer` drops a record that grew a fourth, which is what makes `mcp-server` honestly `PLAINTEXT_BY_DESIGN` rather than a claim the implementation fails to make. It is `LOCAL_ONLY` and `NOT_PORTABLE_BY_DESIGN`: unlike a workflow, which sits there until somebody runs it, a synced or imported server changes the tool surface the model is offered on a machine where nobody added it — every call still confirms, and the person confirming is being asked about a third party they never chose. Adding a server contacts nothing, so a stored server has been named and not trusted. The registrar is the caller the layers beneath were missing: it discovers per server independently, so one unreachable endpoint costs the user nothing from the servers that answered and does not stop startup; it replaces a server's tools rather than merging them, so a tool the server has stopped offering stops existing; and it names a tool whose schema this build will not compile rather than dropping it, because the user's own client may show that tool working. Revocation is free rather than implemented: a tool exists only as a function of the record and the answer the server just gave, and nothing could have pre-approved one, so there is no residual grant. `ToolRegistry.unregister` was added for this and is deliberately narrow — it names a tool, so what stops a caller removing `browser.click` is that there is one caller and it matches the `mcp__<server>__` prefix, which an invariant test counts the way the dispatch and egress call sites are counted. Seven mutants killed: tools merged rather than replaced, a failing server aborting the whole registration, an uncompilable schema dropped silently, the namespace match widened to a bare prefix, a duplicate id overwriting, the stored field set unasserted, and the server count unbounded.
